extracted.intended_audience: poets, translators, literary critics, educated writers and readers interested in diction, taste, and pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for poetic diction, taste formation, translation practice, and reading/teaching performance drawn from Coleridge's literary criticism and footnotes. Emphasizes precision of word-usage, respect for linguistic idioms, cultivation of taste, and humane pedagogical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature or immoderate authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: “With the greatest possible solicitude avoid authorship. Too early or immoderately employed, it makes the head waste and the heart empty; even were there no other worse consequences. A person, who reads only to print, to all probability reads amiss; and he, who sends away through the pen and the press every thought, the moment it occurs to him, will in a short time have sent all away, and will become a mere journeyman of the printing-office, a compositor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish or force into print every passing thought; allow ideas to circulate and be reworked. Beware of living as a mere ‘compositor’ who empties the mind by constant output. Practice restraint to preserve intellectual vigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoughts must be reabsorbed and re-secreted for vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: From the author’s addition: thoughts, like certain secretions, “must be taken up again into the circulation, and be again and again re-secreted to order to ensure a healthful vigour, both to the mind and to its intellectual offspring.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before publication, rework and revisit ideas repeatedly to maintain depth and vitality in writing; value revision and internal digestion of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire good taste by study of the best models
rubrics_metrics.description: “Good taste must be acquired, and like all other good things, is the result of thought and the submissive study of the best models.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To form judgement, study established works whose reputations are matured by the consent of ages. Rely on historically validated exemplars rather than fashionable or untested models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge models by reputations matured into fame
rubrics_metrics.description: “Presume those to be the best, the reputation of which has been matured into fame by the consent of ages. For wisdom always has a final majority, if not by conviction, yet by acquiescence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting exemplars for study, prefer works whose quality has persisted over time; use the canon as a starting point for taste-formation, while still applying critical thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious translating between languages with different idioms
rubrics_metrics.description: “After what I have advanced, it would appear presumption to offer a translation; even if the attempt were not discouraged by the different genius of the English mind and language, which demands a denser body of thought as the condition of a high polish, than the Italian.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that each language has its own poetic idiom and demands: do not expect a straight conversion. Adapt form and density to the target language rather than slavishly mirroring the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precise native equivalents over vague Latin/umbrella terms
rubrics_metrics.description: On rendering Greek/Latin into English: “In almost every instance the precise individual meaning might be given in an English or German word; whereas in Latin we must too often be contented with a mere general and inclusive term.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible use specific native-language words to capture precise meanings rather than relying on broad, vague equivalents. Lexicographical and translational projects should aim for fine-grained synonymy across languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not extend technical words beyond their proper senses (precision of diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the word “scene”: the author objects to any extension of its meaning beyond the theatre sense because it is already equivocal; recommends keeping its original signification full in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clarity by preserving core meanings of words; avoid loose or fashionable generalizations that make diction ambiguous. When a term has a specific theatrical or technical meaning, use it with that reference in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of excessive repetition as a stylistic fault
rubrics_metrics.description: “This sort of repetition is one of this writer’s peculiarities, and there is scarce a page which does not furnish one or more instances...” (followed by many repeated phrases from a play)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and curb unnecessary verbal repetition that weakens expression. Use repetition deliberately and sparingly; excessive reiterated phrases are critiqued as a negative peculiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match metaphors to natural propriety of the image
rubrics_metrics.description: On a misplaced metaphor regarding a wounded stag: the metaphor, though not false, “loses all the propriety of the original” when the position/context changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure metaphors arise naturally from the scene or body language described; a metaphor that fails to align with the physical or contextual reality of the image will feel inappropriate or strained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve important dramatic elements (plot/character fate)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The child is an important personage, for I see not by what possible means the author could have ended the second and third acts but for its timely appearance. How ungrateful then not further to notice its fate!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama (and narrative), once a character or element is introduced as pivotal, the author should account for its ultimate fate or role; unresolved important elements are failures of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force reading-as-speaking in pedagogy; respect distinct modes
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is no less an error in teachers, than a torment to the poor children, to enforce the necessity of reading as they would talk... the child’s tones resemble talking, as far as his fears, tears and trembling will permit. ... an instinctive sense tells the child’s feelings, that to utter its own momentary thoughts, and to recite the written thoughts of another... are two widely different things; and as the two acts are accompanied with widely different feelings, so must they justify different modes of enunciation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching reading or recitation, avoid methods that force textbook-reading to mimic spontaneous speech. Teach distinct modes of enunciation appropriate to speaking versus reciting; avoid humiliating, mechanistic drills that damage natural feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject harsh, punitive public recitation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Joseph Lancaster’s method: “hanging fetters and chains on the child, to the music... one of his school-fellows... dolefully chants out the child’s last speech and confession... this soul-benumbing ignominy... has been extolled as a happy and ingenious method of remedying--what? and how?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pedagogical practices that publicly shame or dehumanize children to enforce conformity. Favor humane, psychologically informed approaches rather than spectacles of humiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value unity and simultaneity of impression over mere condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: On German condensation vs English: though German can condense meaning via compounds, the author suggests the excellence lies in the unity and simultaneousness with which the impression is conveyed, not mere brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for expressive unity — a single, powerful impression — rather than slavishly condensing for economy’s sake. Use language devices appropriate to the target language to achieve vivid simultaneous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard natural conversational phrasing in narrative voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussing Wordsworth: certain phrases are justified only by the narrator’s identity (e.g., a vicar); otherwise, they would be unnatural in ordinary conversation. “Men in general would have said, ‘but that was a circumstance they paid no attention to...’ and the language is, on the theory of the preface, justified only by the narrator’s being the Vicar.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure narrative diction aligns with the narrator’s social identity and speech patterns; avoid archaisms or contrived turns that betray an unnatural voice unless defensible by character perspective.
